newsitem.title: JAPAN: Talks continue on Japan oil rights - Saudi minister.
newsitem.headline: Talks continue on Japan oil rights - Saudi minister.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's Planning Minister Abdul-Wahab bin Abdul-Salam Attar met with members of Japan's energy community on Tuesday, but did not elaborate on Japan's chances for an oil concession renewal in the Neutral Zone.
Japan's Arabian Oil Co Ltd (AOC) has oil production agreements with both Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, which have equally shared mineral rights in the Neutral Zone since its establishment in 1922.
Kuwait has already agreed in principle to renew AOC's drilling rights, which are due to expire in 2003, for another 30 years.
But negotiations for the Saudi concession, which is scheduled to expire in 2000, continues to be a highly sensitive subject between the two countries.
Asked to qualify the likelihood of Saudi Arabia renewing the AOC concession Attar said: "The existing plan extends to the year 2000."
"Currently there are ongoing negotiations between the (Oil) Ministry and the company (AOC)," Attar said.

Speaking at a symposium sponsored by the Committee for Energy Policy Promotion, an arm of the influential business group, the Japan Federation of Economic Organizations (Keidanren), Attar addressed future Japanese investment prospects within Saudi Arabia.
"Saudi Arabia and Japan are bound by ties that have been established over a long period of time," Attar said.

The AOC, which operates about 160 of the Neutral Zone's 614 wells in the Hout and Khafji fields, produces roughly 315,000 barrels per day (bpd) overall, and has plans to raise output to 350,000 bpd by the end of the century.
Any change in Japan's Neutral Zone arrangement would have serious implications for its crude import regime.
The Neutral Zone accounted for some 250,000 bpd of Japan's crude needs in the first quarter of this year, according to statistics from the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI).
That represents a 25,000 bpd gain on the 1996 average.
The Neutral Zone was established by the sultanate of Nejd, now part of Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait, then a British protectorate.
